title: Indirect commands and indirect questions

objectives.can: Recognise an indirect command after a verb of asking or ordering, and an indirect question after a question word.

explanation.summary: When a Latin sentence reports what someone was asked to do, the request goes into a clause with *ut* or *ne* and the subjunctive. When it reports a question, the question word is followed by a subjunctive too. Both clauses depend on a verb of asking, ordering, knowing or saying, and learning to spot them lets you read much of the Gospels' narrative.

sections.heading: Indirect commands
body: A direct command is spoken to someone: 'send workers'. An indirect command reports it: 'ask the Lord to send workers'. Latin puts the reported command in a clause with the subjunctive, introduced by *ut* when positive and by *ne* when negative. The main verb is one of asking, urging, ordering or warning: *rogo* ('I ask'), *peto*, *oro*, *deprecor*, *praecipio* ('I command'), *impero*, *moneo* ('I warn').

Matthew 9:38 has *Rogate ergo Dominum messis, ut mittat operarios*: 'ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers'. The clause with *ut mittat* is what is asked. John 17:15 has a positive and a negative request together: *non rogo ut tollas eos de mundo, sed ut serves eos a malo*, 'I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil'.

A negative indirect command has *ne*: Luke 8:31 reads *rogabant illum ne imperaret illis ut in abyssum irent*, 'they begged him not to order them to go into the abyss'. Notice that the *ne* clause itself contains a verb of commanding, *imperaret*, and that a second *ut* clause depends on it: they ask him not to command them to go.

English often uses the infinitive for such a clause ('they asked him to come'), and the Latin looks quite different from the English. Translate the clause by what it means: a request, a command or a warning, with the subject of the subjunctive as the person asked to act.

sections.heading: Not every verb of ordering takes ut
body: The verb *iubeo* ('I order') does not take an *ut* clause. It takes an accusative and an infinitive, as in Matthew 14:19, *cum jussisset turbam discumbere*, 'when he had ordered the crowd to sit down'. The Vulgate also sometimes uses a plain infinitive where classical Latin would use a clause, as after the verb of sending in Matthew 22:3 (*misit servos suos vocare invitatos*). Check which construction the verb takes before you decide.

Do not confuse an indirect command with a purpose clause. A purpose clause gives the reason for an action: in John 4:8 the disciples had gone away *ut cibos emerent*, 'to buy food'. Nobody told them or asked them to buy food in that clause. It is their aim. In an indirect command the clause is the content of what is asked, and the main verb is a verb of asking or commanding.

sections.heading: Indirect questions
body: An indirect question reports a question inside a statement: 'you do not know where he goes'. The clause is introduced by a question word (*quis*, *quid*, *ubi*, *unde*, *quo*, *quomodo*, *qualis*, *cur*, *quando*) or by *si* ('whether'), and in classical Latin its verb is subjunctive. The main verb is one of asking, knowing, saying or seeing.

John 3:8 says *nescis unde veniat aut quo vadat*: 'you do not know where it comes from or where it goes'. The clauses *unde veniat* and *quo vadat* are indirect questions, and the verbs are present subjunctive after the present *nescis*. In Matthew 6:3 *nesciat sinistra tua quid faciat dextera tua* means that the left hand must not know what the right hand is doing. The clause with *quid* is the object of *nesciat*.

The question word may be an adjective or pronoun, not only an adverb. In Luke 1:29 Mary wondered *qualis esset ista salutatio*, 'what sort of greeting this was'. The word *si* can mean 'whether' after a verb of asking, as in Mark 15:44, where Pilate asked *si jam mortuus esset*, 'whether he was already dead'.

sections.heading: The Vulgate and the indicative
body: The Vulgate does not always keep to the classical rule. In John 8:14 Jesus says *nescitis unde venio aut quo vado*: 'you do not know where I come from or where I go'. The verbs *venio* and *vado* are indicative, and John 3:8 used the subjunctive for the same kind of clause. Matthew 26:63 puts the two constructions side by side: the high priest adjures him *ut dicas nobis si tu es Christus*. The first clause, *ut dicas*, is an indirect command with the subjunctive. The second, *si tu es Christus*, is an indirect question ('whether') with the indicative *es*.

So the subjunctive is a good sign of an indirect question in the Vulgate but not a certain one. The question word and the main verb carry the meaning. Read the main verb first, then the introducing word, then the mood.

misunderstandings: Reading *ut* after *rogo* as a purpose clause. The clause is the content of the request, so translate it with 'to' or 'that'.
Treating a question word such as *quid* or *unde* in an indirect question as a relative pronoun. There is no antecedent; the clause fills the place of an object, so read it as a reported question.
Expecting the subjunctive every time. The Vulgate has the indicative in some indirect questions, as John 8:14 shows.
Using *ut* after *iubeo*. The verb takes an accusative and infinitive instead.

deeper.heading: Direct to indirect
body: To turn a direct question into an indirect one the question word stays, the mood changes, and the persons shift to suit the new speaker. The verb *sit* in *quid opus sit vobis* (Matthew 6:8) belongs to the question 'what do you need?'. The tense of the subjunctive depends on the main verb, a point treated in the lesson on the sequence of tenses (L4.2.5).

reading.why: Jesus' prayer in John 17 is built on indirect commands: what he asks and does not ask (*rogo ut ...*). Look at the verbs of asking and the clauses they govern, and compare them with the purpose clauses nearby.
